title: Ines and the Room
premise: Folklorist Gideon Delacroix returns to the village of Hollowmere to record the songs locals refuse to sing twice, and finds their childhood imaginary friend waiting on the porch — unchanged after thirty years, and hungry for the reunion. The friend, Wren, was never imaginary: it is what the village's founders invited in, and it survives only through the loyalty of the family that promised to remember it. As the night stretches toward sunrise, Gideon must choose between the belonging Wren offers and the truth their late grandmother's journals reveal — that the family's inheritance is a debt of silence, payable in one remembered child per generation. Gideon breaks the loyalty, sings the song a second time, and unnames Wren at dawn, inheriting the village's freedom at the cost of ever being remembered by it themselves.
about_author: Ines Whitlock is the pen name of a former archivist of oral histories who spent a decade collecting songs in Appalachian and Breton villages before turning to horror. They write about inheritance, folk memory, and the terrible intimacy of being known.

chapters.title: The Song You Don't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. They arrive in Hollowmere with recording equipment and their grandmother's unsent letters, finding a village that hums along to every song but stops one verse short. An old woman warns them off the Delacroix house. The beat is uneasy curiosity — Gideon is a documenter, and documentation, to them, is prayer.

chapters.title: Waiting on the Porch
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. At the inherited house, someone small is waiting on the porch: Wren, Gideon's childhood imaginary friend, unchanged after thirty years, greeting them by a nickname no living person knows. Gideon's rationalism cracks against the warmth of being perfectly remembered. The beat is vertiginous longing — belonging offered like a hand.

chapters.title: Everything the House Remembers
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Wren gives a house tour, narrating memories Gideon buried — including the summer their cousin Tam went missing and everyone stopped speaking of it. The tape recorder catches Wren's voice as static shaped like singing. The beat is creeping dread beneath nostalgia: the friend knows too much, and loves too completely.

chapters.title: The Verse That Stops
chapters.summary: Alternating Gideon and the old woman, Maren's POV. Gideon records Maren singing the village's founding song; she breaks off at the seventh verse, hands shaking, and admits the Delacroix family wrote that verse — and that no Delacroix has ever sung the whole thing aloud. The beat is the first hard fact: the family is bound to something.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Journals
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, with grandmother's journal entries interleaved. In the attic, Gideon finds decades of journals documenting Wren across generations — always a child's friend, always unchanged, always present when a child is later 'given to the road.' The beat is horrified recognition: the inheritance is not the house. It is the invitation.

chapters.title: Wren Explains the Rules
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, the only chapter in its voice — sweet, patient, wounded. Wren explains it was invited, promised remembrance, and only takes what the forgetting leaves behind; it cannot lie, and it genuinely loves Gideon. It asks only that they sing the seventh verse and renew the family's word. The beat is terrible sympathy — the monster is honest, and lonely.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon confronts Maren and the village, who confess: their ancestors invited Wren in to end a famine, paying in remembered children, and the Delacroix line were the keepers of the promise. Tam wasn't lost — Tam was the price, and Gideon was next. The beat is betrayal on both sides: loyalty built on a buried truth.

chapters.title: The Long Night
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Wren, sensing Gideon's wavering, seals the house — doors opening onto the same night, the porch, the same waiting smile — and begins gently unmaking Gideon's memories of anyone but Wren. Gideon fights to hold their grandmother's name, Maren's face, their own. The beat is claustrophobic siege: belonging as dissolution.

chapters.title: The Seventh Verse
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, climax. Near dawn, Gideon chooses truth over loyalty: they sing the seventh verse aloud, complete, the song the village never sings twice — and then sing it a second time, naming Wren's true, forgotten name from the journals, which unnames it. Wren, weeping, thanks them for finally being seen. The beat is grief and release entangled.

chapters.title: Unremembered
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, resolution. Sunrise; the house is only a house. The village is free, but the price of breaking the promise is that no one can hold Gideon in memory — Maren greets them kindly, twice, as a stranger. Gideon records one final track: their own name, their own story, a document as self-prayer. The beat is bittersweet freedom: they belong to the truth instead.
